title: A groundnut farmer after the reforms
body: Ramaiah grows groundnut on a small plot in a drought-prone district. Before the reforms he spent about Rs 10,000 per season on seeds, fertilisers, labour and bullock power, and sold two quintals at Rs 7,000 per quintal. In recent years no major irrigation project has been started in his district, and research and extension services that once helped farmers fight crop disease have shrunk because of lower public expenditure. The subsidy on fertilisers and seeds has been partly withdrawn, so his cost of cultivation has risen. At the same time, the removal of restrictions on imports has filled local markets with cheap imported edible oils, and Ramaiah often cannot get a price for his groundnut that covers his cost.
